passages.happening:
‘Then Job answered’ (verse 1). “How you have helped the powerless and saved the arm that is feeble! How you have counseled the unwise and provided fully sound insight!” (verses 2-3).

“To whom have you uttered these words? And whose spirit spoke through you?” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Bildad's short speech was the friends' last word. Job answers it, and this reply opens a long section in which he speaks alone, through chapter 31.

The you in these verses is singular in Hebrew, presumably Bildad. The sarcasm is plain. Bildad has helped no one. And Job asks where Bildad's words came from: whose spirit was speaking?
passages.asks: Job asked Bildad whom his words had helped. Ask that of your own last piece of advice to someone in trouble. And ask whose spirit your words came from.

passages.happening:
The dead tremble beneath the waters. “Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering” (verse 6).

“He stretches out the north over empty space; He hangs the earth upon nothing. He wraps up the waters in His clouds, yet the clouds do not burst under their own weight” (verses 7-8). He covers the face of the moon, marks the horizon on the waters at the edge of light and darkness, and the pillars of heaven tremble at his rebuke. ‘By His power He stirred the sea; by His understanding He shattered Rahab. By His breath the skies were cleared; His hand pierced the fleeing serpent’ (verses 12-13).

“Indeed, these are but the fringes of His ways; how faint is the whisper we hear of Him! Who then can understand the thunder of His power?” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Bildad praised God's power in six verses. Job praises it in ten, with far greater range. He does not need to be taught that God is great. He knows it better than the friends do, and that is exactly what makes his suffering so hard to understand.

The hymn climbs from the depths upward. The dead in verse 5 are the rephaim, a poetic word for the shades of the dead, pictured beneath the waters. Sheol and Abaddon, destruction, are two names for the realm of the dead, and even it lies open before God. The poetry uses the picture of the world shared across the ancient Near East, an earth over the waters, a horizon at the sea's edge and heaven on pillars, as a way of speaking about God's rule over everything.

Rahab here is not the woman of Jericho. It is a poetic name for a sea monster of chaos. Clay tablets from Ugarit, a Canaanite city destroyed around 1200 BC, tell of the storm god fighting the Sea and a monster called the fleeing serpent. Job uses the same phrase to say that the powers other peoples feared or worshiped are subject to God.

Verse 14 is one of the book's great lines. All of this is only the edge of God's ways, a whisper. The hymn looks ahead to God's own speeches in chapters 38 to 41.
passages.later: Isaiah uses the same name for the monster God will defeat: ‘the LORD will take His sharp, great, and mighty sword, and bring judgment on Leviathan the fleeing serpent’ (Isaiah 27:1).
passages.hard:
Does verse 7, He hangs the earth upon nothing, show scientific knowledge ahead of its time?

Some readers have seen in verse 7 an anticipation of modern astronomy, since the earth does float in space without any physical support. Others point out that the same poem speaks of the pillars of heaven (verse 11; the BSB has foundations) and of a horizon drawn on the waters (verse 10), which reflect the ancient picture of the world rather than a modern one. On this view the line means that the earth rests on nothing but God's power, a statement about God using the imagery of its time. A middle position holds that the verse makes no scientific claim but still says something true that fits what is now known: the world is upheld by God and by no other foundation.

Most interpreters agree that the poem's purpose is not to teach how the world is built but to lead to worship, which is exactly where verse 14 takes it.
passages.asks: Job said that all he could see of God was the edge of his ways. Ask what you have seen of God's ways, and how small it is beside the whole. And ask whether knowing that makes you humbler or more afraid, or both.
